summary: Describes the Network File System protocol, which Sun Microsystems and others were already using, so that others may benefit from it. It also discusses some design issues, and notes that a new version of the protocol was under development. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: NFS version two lets a client ask a remote server to look up, read, write, or change files. It uses shared data formats so different kinds of computers can exchange those requests. The server keeps little protocol state, which helps clients recover by retrying.

subtitle: The remote procedures and file handles used by NFS version two.

tldr.problem: A computer needs a way to access files stored on another machine across different operating systems and network types.
tldr.mechanism: NFS version two defines remote procedures carried using Sun RPC and XDR. Its server is designed to keep little protocol state, allowing clients to retry requests after interruptions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1094 documents a protocol already used by Sun Microsystems and others. It is Informational, and the RFC said a newer version was under development at the time.

today: RFC 1094 is an Informational description of NFS version two, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC said a newer NFS version was under development when it was written.

sections.title: What NFS Provides
sections.content:
The Network File System (NFS) protocol provides remote access to shared files across a network. The RFC describes version two and aims to work across different machines, operating systems, network architectures, and transport protocols.

NFS uses Remote Procedure Call (RPC) operations and eXternal Data Representation (XDR) to describe requests and data. A separate mount protocol handles operating-system-specific setup and gives a client its first file handle.
sections.plainLanguage: NFS lets a client request file operations from another computer. RPC carries the requests, and XDR gives the data a shared representation.

sections.title: Stateless Servers and File Handles
sections.content:
The RFC aims for servers that do not need to retain protocol state about clients. When a connection or server fails, a client can retry a request rather than rebuild the server's session state. Operations are made repeatable where possible, though the RFC identifies some directory changes as potentially non-idempotent.

Files are unstructured byte streams in a hierarchical directory tree. The client looks up one path component at a time, and file operations use an opaque file handle that contains whatever information the server needs to identify a file.
sections.plainLanguage: The server does not need to remember a conversation with each client. Each request carries the information needed for the operation, including a handle that identifies the file.

sections.title: NFS Procedures
sections.content:
NFS version two defines procedures for reading attributes, looking up names, reading and writing files, changing directories, and getting file-system information. A lookup returns a file handle and attributes; a read returns data from an offset; and a write stores data at an offset.

Calls are synchronous: when a procedure returns, the client can assume the operation has completed, and a successful write is on stable storage. Replies include a status value indicating success or an error. The RFC marks the ROOT procedure obsolete and reserves WRITECACHE for a later revision.
sections.plainLanguage: The procedure list is a menu of file operations. A reply reports whether the operation succeeded, and a completed write is treated as safely stored.

sections.title: Permissions and Transport
sections.content:
NFS does not strictly define server permission checking. The RFC expects servers to use operating-system checks based on credentials such as the client's user ID, group ID, and groups. Because a stateless server does not know which files are open, it checks permissions on each read and write.

The RFC says NFS normally uses UDP and gives UDP port 2049, noting that this port was not officially assigned. The separate mount service can use UDP or TCP, and its port is found through the server's portmapper.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks the client's supplied identity information when it handles each operation. NFS normally uses UDP in this RFC, while the separate mount service can use UDP or TCP.

sections.title: Limits, Retries, and Mounting
sections.content:
The RFC sets a maximum of 8192 bytes for data in a READ or WRITE request, 1024 bytes for a pathname, 255 bytes for a file name, and 32 bytes for a file handle. It notes that smaller transfer sizes may work better on slower networks or through gateways.

A soft mount can return an error after optional retransmissions; a hard mount continues retransmitting. The separate mount protocol obtains the first file handle and can list or remove mount records. Its mount list is advisory rather than necessary for NFS correctness.
sections.plainLanguage: NFS sets limits on request data and names. Clients can be configured to stop retrying after failures or continue retrying, and the mount protocol obtains the first file handle.
